raw_text:
### Introduction
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a leading cause of mortality globally, representing a significant public health challenge. For decades, the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has served as the cornerstone of both primary and secondary prevention of life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias. However, the intravascular and intracardiac placement of TV-ICD leads introduces long-term vulnerabilities, including venous thrombosis, lead fracture, tricuspid valve regurgitation, and systemic bloodstream infections [1,2]. Managing these complications often necessitates high-risk lead extraction procedures. To bypass the risks associated with indwelling transvenous hardware, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed, offering an entirely extra-thoracic alternative [3].

### System Design and Patient Screening
The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator placed in a subcutaneous or intermuscular pocket on the left lateral thoracic wall and a single subcutaneous lead positioned parasternally [4,5]. Unlike TV-ICDs, which sense cardiac electrical activity via direct intracardiac contact, the S-ICD uses far-field sensing configurations. Because of this, S-ICD sensing is vulnerable to cardiac and non-cardiac oversensing. Consequently, rigorous pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening is mandatory to verify that the patient's native QRS-T complex morphology does not promote T-wave oversensing (TWO) or other sensing anomalies [6]. The manual screening tool utilizes three vectors to ensure adequate signal-to-noise ratios [7]. The subsequent introduction of automated screening tools has significantly improved the efficiency of patient selection, expanding the eligible population [8].

### Clinical Evidence and Efficacy
The clinical efficacy and safety of the S-ICD have been rigorously evaluated in numerous registries and trials. Early real-world registries, such as the EFFORTLESS registry, and the initial Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial, confirmed high efficacy in detecting and terminating ventricular fibrillation (VF) during induced and spontaneous episodes [9,10]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized controlled trial to directly compare S-ICD and TV-ICD [11]. It established that the S-ICD is non-inferior to the TV-ICD with respect to a composite primary endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks. The subsequent UNTOUCHED trial, which evaluated S-ICD in a primary prevention cohort with low ejection fraction, demonstrated exceptionally low inappropriate shock rates due to high-rate programming and advanced detection algorithms [12]. Long-term observational data have confirmed stable, durable outcomes over multi-year follow-ups, with defibrillation efficacy remaining consistently high [13].

### Procedural Aspects and Complications
The surgical technique for S-ICD implantation has evolved. Initially, the device was positioned in a subcutaneous pocket, which was associated with discomfort and cosmetic concerns. The transition to the intermuscular pocket technique—placing the generator between the latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior muscles—has improved cosmetic outcomes and reduced device erosion rates [14,15]. While S-ICD avoids lead-related vascular complications [16], inappropriate shocks remain a major clinical challenge, primarily driven by T-wave oversensing or skeletal muscle noise [17]. To mitigate this, manufacturers developed the "Smart Pass" filter, a high-pass software filter that attenuates the low-frequency signals typical of T-waves without compromising QRS detection [18,19]. However, because the S-ICD cannot deliver chronic pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP), clinicians must exclude patients with established pacing indications [20].

### Special Patient Populations
The S-ICD is highly advantageous for several distinct patient cohorts. It is the preferred therapy for young patients with channelopathies, long QT syndrome, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), who face a lifetime of cumulative TV-ICD lead wear and potential extraction risks [21,22]. Additionally, the S-ICD is an excellent option for patients with limited venous access, congenital heart disease, or those at high risk for systemic infection, such as individuals with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis [23,24,25]. Clinical registries highlight that S-ICD delivers reliable shocks in heart failure cohorts without compromised performance [26].

### Future Frontiers and Modular Systems
To overcome the lack of ATP and pacing capabilities, modular cardiac rhythm management systems are currently being developed. These innovative configurations pair the extra-thoracic S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LCP) implanted directly into the right ventricle [27,28]. When the S-ICD detects monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, it can wirelessly communicate with the LCP to deliver ATP, potentially terminating the arrhythmia painlessly and avoiding unnecessary shocks [29]. Continued technological iterations, including improved battery longevity and device miniaturization, will further solidify the S-ICD's role in cardiac electrophysiology [30].
